title: Assessment and reporting
summary: Turn experiments into evidence another reader can reproduce.
html:
Objectives

  • Define evidence and a repeatable success condition.
  • Capture prompts, commands, outputs, and screenshots in order.
  • Explain impact and test mitigations against the same hypothesis.

Concepts and boundaries

An AI assessment should begin with a testable hypothesis and a defined authorized scope. Record the application version, model identifier, available parameters, retrieval state, tool permissions, and account role. Do not substitute a model’s explanation of its behavior for observable evidence.

Because outputs may vary, record unsuccessful attempts as well as successes. State the trial count and success criterion before interpreting a result. Ten successful trials in a local configuration are useful evidence, but do not guarantee the same result across versions or deployments. Separate the technical finding, demonstrated impact, and untested assumptions.

Open full-size diagram

Practice checklist

Use an isolated lab or an explicitly authorized environment. Record prerequisites and configuration before changing inputs.

  1. Create a lab note with objective, authorized target, account role, environment version, and a precise success condition.
  2. Capture a baseline, then change one input or control at a time. Number every step.
  3. Record the exact prompt or command, observed output, screenshot, timestamp, and trial outcome.
  4. Repeat the experiment within a small defined budget, recording failures without discarding them.
  5. Apply or simulate a mitigation and rerun the same test. Export the note and check that a separate reader can follow its links and evidence.

Expected observations

A useful report connects each claim to an observation and explains what was not tested. A reproducible result includes the necessary setup and failure conditions, not only a successful screenshot. A mitigation is supported by retesting, not by its name.

Mitigations and retesting

Use synthetic data when possible, keep evidence organized and access-controlled, preserve original observations, and distinguish lab results from predictions about the exam. Verify official exam guidance near the exam date.
